question: For the infinite series \[ \begin{aligned} &1-\dfrac12-\dfrac14+\dfrac18\\ &{}-\dfrac1{16}-\dfrac1{32}+\dfrac1{64}\\ &{}-\dfrac1{128}-\cdots, \end{aligned} \] let \(S\) be the (limiting) sum. Then \(S\) equals:
solution:
The signs repeat in groups of three: positive, negative, negative. Each new group is \(1/8\) times the preceding group, so consecutive triples reveal a geometric pattern. For \(k=0,1,2,\ldots\), a triple has sum
\[
\left(\frac18\right)^k
\left(1-\frac12-\frac14\right)
=\frac14\left(\frac18\right)^k.
\]
Let \(P_N\) be the sum of the first \(N\) terms. For a positive integer \(m\), the first \(3m\) terms form \(m\) complete triples. The finite geometric sum formula gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
P_{3m}
&=\frac14\left(1+\frac18+\cdots+
\left(\frac18\right)^{m-1}\right)\\
&=\frac27\left(1-\left(\frac18\right)^m\right).
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(0<1/8<1\), the power \((1/8)^m\) tends to zero. Hence these partial sums tend to \(2/7\).

We must also account for partial sums that stop inside a triple. After \(3m\) terms, the sum of the magnitudes of the next two terms is
\[
\left(\frac18\right)^m\left(1+\frac12\right),
\]
which tends to zero. Thus stopping after one or two additional terms has no effect on the limiting sum. All partial sums therefore approach
\[
S=\boxed{\frac27},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).

edges.reason: The geometric definition compares consecutive indexed terms by a fixed nonzero ratio, so sequence and consecutive-term meanings are necessary.

The source defines a nonzero consecutive-term quotient. The new series uses power-form terms, including a=0 or r=0 where that quotient is unavailable. Nonzero geometric sequences are useful preparation, but the source quotient-based definition is not a universal prerequisite for the broader series scope.

edges.reason: Taking the limit of the finite sum is the standard derivation and supports the convergence check. Applying a/(1-r) under |r|<1 can also be justified by self-similarity S=a+rS once convergence is known.
